ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Loading catalyst nanoparticles onto polymer fibers for the removal of indoor pollutants such as HCHO encounters many problems such as uneven distribution, active site coverage, high cost and environmental pollution. Here we efficiently loaded MnO2 on the surface of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) fibers (MnO2@PET) within 10 s by utilizing the friction heat and mechanical action generated between MnO2 and PET fibers during rapid stirring. The thickness of the MnO2 coating ranged from ∼0.14 µm to 2.19 µm. After initial weight loss of 10.2 ∼ 10.4% in the first 30 min, the composite fibers remained stable weight in the later 150 min during ultrasonic oscillation, indicating the durability and fastness of the MnO2 coating. As-synthesized MnO2@PET composites enabled superior HCHO removal rate (95.5%) and conversion to CO2 (75.5%) within 120 min at room temperature, and it can be easily regenerated at low temperature (60 °C).

ce:section.ce:para: Formaldehyde (HCHO), an omnipresent indoor contaminant, has aroused serious concern due to its continuous emission from various furniture and decoration materials [1,2]. Even a low concentration of HCHO may bring severe harm to human respiratory tract, nervous system and skin disease, and increase the morbidity of cancer [3]. In a variety of strategies raised for HCHO abatement, the room-temperature oxidation into innoxious CO2 by heterogeneous catalysts (e. g. noble metal-based catalysts and transition metal oxides) is a most effective approach with superior capability and low energy consumption [4,5].

It is well known that noble metal-based catalysts (Pt, Au, Ag) generally display excellent activity for HCHO decomposition at room temperature [6–8]. Besides, transition metal oxides such as MnO2 present room-temperature activity in the catalytic oxidation of HCHO [9,10]. Dai et al. [11] reported that δ-MnO2 with plentiful manganese defects effectively oxidized HCHO into CO2 and H2O under normal temperature. Chen et al. [12] compared the activity of four types of MnO2 crystal phases, i.e. α-, β-, γ-, and δ-MnO2, of which δ-MnO2 exhibited the best performance. Ji et al. [13] investigated the effect of potassium (K+) concentrations in δ-MnO2 on its activity for HCHO removal. Wang et al. [14] found that the interlayer water in δ-MnO2 was dominant in HCHO removal rather than the specific surface area. A high efficient 3D-MnO2 framework was fabricated, which exhibited exceptional catalytic activity for 100 ppm of HCHO under gas hourly space velocity (GHSV) of 180 L/ (gcat h) at room temperature [15].

Although many highly active MnO2 catalysts have been successfully synthesized, they cannot be directly used in practical application and are usually loaded on the carrier in the form of particles for subsequent catalytic oxidation. Sekine et al. [16] prepared an air-cleaning board by loading 77% of commercial MnO2 and activated carbon particles on a fiber cloth through adhesives, which could continuously convert HCHO into CO2 and H2O during seven months. Liu et al. [17] adopted an ice-templating method to assemble 2D MnO2 nanosheets into organic-free MnO2 aerogels with supper low density, strong oxidation capacity and effective adsorption of toxic reducing gases. Dai et al. [18] introduced a strategy of low temperature atomic layer deposition (ALD) to create an oxide thin film on the surface of polypropylene (PP) filter, and then MnO2 nanoparticles were grown in situ on its surface.

The loading of catalyst nanoparticles onto the surface of supporting substances faces many problems such as coverage of active sites, mechanical stability and high production cost. Thus, it is of great interest and significance to load catalyst nanoparticles efficiently and economically while keeping their high activity [11]. Here we report a facile method to coat MnO2 nanoparticles onto the surface of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) melt-blown fibers, which has the advantages of high surface area, outstanding elastic recovery, strong strength, ease of mass production and low cost [19,20]. To date, direct loading of MnO2 catalyst nanoparticles on PET fibers without binder has not been reported. One of the obstacles is that MnO2 nanoparticles are apt to agglomeration, which will lead to load heterogeneity. Another reason is that the chemically inert PET fiber restricts its chemical combination with MnO2 [21]. Here a green and efficient strategy was adopted to join MnO2 nanoparticles and PET fibers via friction-heating and mechanical action, which achieved the relatively uniform loading of MnO2 on PET fiber surface and preserved active sites of MnO2 catalyst. As a result, these MnO2-coated PET fibers exhibit remarkable removal capability for HCHO at room temperature. This loading method is energy-saving and environmentally friendly, hence it presents promising possibility to load a variety of nanoparticles on similar polymer fibers.

Manganese dioxide (MnO2) powder (40/60 meshes), a catalyst for the oxidation of formaldehyde (HCHO), was supplied by Nanjing Yujie Environmental Technology Co., Ltd. Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) staple fibers with various diameters of 7, 15, 20 and 30 µm from SIBAOTE Co., Ltd. were used as substrates for the loading of MnO2.

Prior to the MnO2 loading, PET fibers were placed in the blender (FW1000, China) and loosened into a fluffy state after starting the device for 20 s. Then the fluffy PET fibers (2.0 g) and 0.3 g of MnO2 powder were placed in the blender and stirred at 24,000 r/min for 5 s. Next, after manually mix the powder and fibers, operate the device again for another 5 s to complete the first loading. After the first loading was completed, a new batch of 0.3 g of MnO2 powder was added in this blender to repeat the above procedure. Using this efficient process, MnO2 crystals were firmly loaded onto the surface of PET fibers, and the composite materials were obtained. Hereafter, MnO2@PET-diameter (e. g. MnO2@PET-7 µm) denotes loading MnO2 twice on the surface of polyethylene terephthalate fibers with different diameters. PET and MnO2@PET-loading times (e. g. MnO2@PET-4) represent raw polyethylene terephthalate fibers and the composite fibers loaded with MnO2 for different loading times, respectively.

Tests of material properties were performed in the light of our earlier reported methods [15,22,23]. X-ray diffraction (XRD, D8-Advance, Germany) was recorded from 2θ = 5°-90° at the scan rate of 8°/min with a Cu Kα radiation source (λ = 0.1542 nm). Field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM, Hitachi S5500, Japan) was conducted to observe the surface morphology of specimens.

Attenuation total reflection Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR, Model Nicolet 870, America), over the spectral range from 4000 to 400 cm−1 at a resolution of 4 cm−1, was used to analyze the surface functional groups. The Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET, ASAP 2020, America), revealing the distribution of mesopores or micropores via collecting nitrogen adsorption–desorption isotherms at 77 K, were determined to achieve the specific surface area. The macropore distribution was assessed by mercury porosimeter (Micromeritics AutoPore Iv 9510, America). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, ESCALAB 250Xi, America), adopting Al Kα as X-ray excitation source, was examined to analyze the chemical states of the surface elements. Binding energies needed to be calibrated for surface charging based on the energy of the C 1 s peak at 284.8 eV, and the proportion of elements with different valence states is calculated in line with the peak area.

In-situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectrometry (DRIFTS, Nicolet 6700, America), collected with a resolution ratio of 4 cm−1 and a cumulation of 32 scans, was performed to appraise the intermediate products in the oxidation process of HCHO, in which reaction gas mixture (∼30 ppm of HCHO and O2) was introduced into the in-situ cell at a 35 mL/min flow rate at room temperature. 1H MAS NMR spectra were recorded using a solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR, JNM-ECZ600R, Japan) spectrometer.

Adhesive strength of MnO2 layer was measured via ultrasonic oscillation. 2.0 g of composite material samples were placed in beakers containing deionized water and subjected to ultrasonic oscillation (KH-300DE, China) under the condition of 300 W, 40 kHz and room temperature for 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180 min, respectively. Then they were dried at 105 °C in oven and weighted. This method measures the adhesive strength based on weight loss rate, which was calculated according to the Eq. (1).

We assessed the HCHO removal activity of materials in two ways: static and dynamic test. As for the static test, the catalytic activity of samples was evaluated in a cuboid plexiglass reactor with the volume of 4.0 L. 50 mg of catalyst powder or 2.0 g of composite material specimens was placed in a glass Petri dish with a glass cover-plate. The Petri dish containing specimens was located at the bottom of the reactor, followed by an injection of ∼ 15 µL of HCHO solution into it. Under the mixing by the fan in the reactor, HCHO gradually volatilized until its concentration maintained at ∼ 200 ppm. Subsequently, the glass cover-plate was removed to expose the sample to the HCHO gas. The reaction temperature was stable at room temperature (25 ± 2 °C). For the cyclic experiments, the first-test sample was further tested as above until the sixth test was finished. Finally, the sixth-test sample was regenerated at 60 °C in air for 120 min, followed by the above activity test. HCHO removal efficiency was calculated according to Eq. (2).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Morphology, structure and catalytic activity of MnO2 powder
ce:section.ce:para:
X-ray diffraction (XRD) in Fig. 1
a is used to probe the crystalline phases of MnO2 powder, which exhibited four weak diffraction peaks around 11.9˚, 25.1˚, 37.2˚ and 66.3˚, corresponding to (001), (002), (100) and (110) of δ-MnO2 [25]. The weak intensity indicated the relatively poor crystallinity and many defects, which just proved the effectiveness of as-received MnO2 powder in removing HCHO. Besides, the lattice distance of 0.24 nm corresponding to the (110) facet was observed in the high-resolution TEM image (Fig. 1 d) [26]. From Fig. 1 b, high magnification SEM image clearly reveals that the MnO2 powder consists of irregular lamellar structure with the sizes of 23–85 nm that was obtained by measuring more than 50 different lateral sizes of the exposed sheets. These nanosheets agglomerated into nanoparticles with sizes of 200–600 nm through the interaction of weak van der Waals forces, which is confirmed by the TEM image (Fig. 1 c).

The chemical state and contents of Mn and O elements were checked with X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). The average oxidation state (AOS) of Mn was calculated according to the binding energy difference (ΔE) of Mn 3 s in XPS through an empirical formula, i.e. AOS = 8.956 – 1.126 ×ΔE [27]. After the curve-fitting of Mn 2p3/2 (Fig. 2
a) [28], the ratio of Mn3+ (∼641.8 eV) to Mn4+ (∼643.4 eV) is 1.59, which is in line with the average oxidation state (3.43) obtained from Mn 3 s (Fig. 2 b) [29]. Generally, larger amount of Mn3+ means rich oxygen vacancies in MnO2, which promotes the generation of reactive oxygen species on the surface decomposing HCHO [30]. Additionally, the deconvoluted O 1 s spectra (Fig. 2 c) manifest two peaks at 529.5 eV and 531.1 eV, which were assigned to the lattice oxygen (Olatt) and the surface adsorbed oxygen (Oads), respectively [31,32]. The ratio of Oads/Olatt is 0.93, indicating the existence of abundant Oads. It is well-known that Oads species play a significant role in the catalytic oxidation activity at low temperature [33–36]. Therefore, these results imply that this MnO2 powder might have high activity for HCHO decomposition. As shown in Fig. 2 d, in the static HCHO removal test, 50 mg MnO2 powder could remove 91.2% of ∼ 200 ppm HCHO within 120 min at room temperature, and simultaneously CO2 were generated. Nearly 60.5% HCHO were transformed into CO2 within 160 min. The difference between HCHO removal and conversion to CO2 suggested the incomplete oxidation of HCHO at room temperature. This can be ascribed to accumulation of the HCHO oxidation intermediates such as carbonate and formate species on the surface of MnO2 powder.

To verify this postulation, the in situ HCHO oxidation on the surface of MnO2 powder was investigated with the diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectrometry (DRIFTS). The MnO2 powder was exposed to a flow of ∼ 30 ppm HCHO/O2 for 60 min at room temperature. As shown in Fig. 3 , the absorption peak at 1570 cm−1 revealed the formation of hydrogen-bonded HCOOH [37], and this peak decreased gradually and even disappeared with time-on-stream. This might be because the generated HCOOH was unstable and easily converted into formate (HCOO–) species. The peaks at 1350 cm−1, 1608 cm−1 and 2827 cm−1 could be ascribed to formate species, while the peak at 1680 cm−1 was assigned to bridging carbonate species [4,6,35,38]. The intensities of these peaks increased with the exposure time, indicating that HCHO could be oxidized to formate and carbonate and some of these species accumulated on the surface of MnO2. In addition, the intensity of the peak at 1464 cm−1, assigned to dioxymethylene species (DOM) originating from the oxidation of HCHO to formate species, was relatively weak, indicating the rapid conversion of DOM [15,39]. The negative peaks around 3681 cm−1 and 1257 cm−1 suggested the consumption of surface hydroxyl groups [40,41].

The cross-section and longitudinal morphology of PET fiber before and after MnO2 loading are shown in Fig. 4 . The raw PET fibers had the smooth surface with approximately circular cross-section, about 7.42 µm in diameter (Fig. 4 a), and it became coarse after loaded with MnO2 powder (Fig. 4 b). The optical photos in Fig. 4 c and 4d show the color change from white of the raw PET to dark brown, indicating that high content of MnO2 was effectively loaded onto the PET fibers.

The morphologies of MnO2@PET loaded with different times are shown in Fig. 5 , and the corresponding mass fraction of MnO2 on the PET fibers and the average diameter of MnO2@PET are listed in Table 1 . The average diameter of composites was obtained by measuring more than 50 different positions of MnO2@PET. The loaded amount of MnO2 almost reached the maximum after 5 times loading, while the diameter of MnO2 loaded PEF fibers increased in the first 3 times and then kept constant due to the agglomeration or compaction of MnO2 nanoparticles. SEM images in Fig. 5 show the similar rough surface morphology including scattered smaller sizes and tightly packed MnO2 particles with larger size, manifesting that MnO2 particles were dispersed by blades in the blender and simultaneously packed during the loading process. Among them, MnO2@PET-2 (Fig. 5 b-5e) exhibited relatively uniform loading with favorable dispersion of MnO2 particles on the fiber surface, which is beneficial to expose more active sites of MnO2 catalyst. With the increase of the loading times, MnO2 particles became densely packed on the surface of fiber, and agglomeration occurred to a large extent (Fig. 5 g-5l), which is consistent with the change of PET diameters. Moreover, the individual particles of MnO2 on the fiber surface were significantly reduced due to the compaction after 5 and 6 times loading.

The SEM images of MnO2@PET-2 cross section (Fig. 6
a-6c) give insight into the thickness of the MnO2 coating, which was not very even, ranging from ∼ 0.14 µm to 2.19 µm. To verify the adhesive strength of MnO2 particles on the PET fibers, the MnO2@PET-2 composite was sonicated. As shown in Fig. 6 d, though after the first 30 min ultrasonic oscillation, there was 10.2 ∼ 10.4% of weight loss in MnO2@PET-2 composites, it kept stable in the later 150 min, indicating the residual MnO2 coating was closely bounded on the PET fibers. As shown from the inset of Fig. 6 d, the agglomerated nanoparticles on the surface of fiber in MnO2@PET-2 fell off after the ultrasonic oscillation, while most of the remaining MnO2 nanoparticles still remained firmly bonded to the fiber surface. Besides, the XRD patters (Fig. 1 a) revealed the crystal structure of MnO2 nanoparticles did not change after loading.

The N2 adsorption–desorption isotherms and the relevant pore-size distribution curves are shown in Fig. 7
a and 7b. The raw PET fibers owned extremely low specific surface area (1.7 m2/g), which was mostly contributed by small amount of mesoporous (∼ 4.57 nm) (Fig. 7 b) generated during the fiber pretreatment. The adsorption isotherm of MnO2 powder (Fig. 7 a) can be attributed to the type IV, implying the existence of interconnected mesopores. MnO2 powder possessed a wide range of pore-size distribution, which resulted in relatively high specific surface area (85.8 m2/g). After the loading of MnO2 powder, MnO2@PET-2 exhibited a pore-size distribution between 3.1 ∼ 10.5 nm and specific surface area of 26.3 m2/g, which could be ascribed to the loaded MnO2 particles. Moreover, the mercury intrusion determination (Fig. 8 ) indicates the presence of many big pores with the size of several micrometers in the MnO2@PET-2, some of them were obviously smaller than those observed in PET fibers, confirming the coating of MnO2 particles on the fibers. It is worth noting that MnO2@PET-2 did not contain the pores among 361 ∼ 954 nm of MnO2 particles, which might be caused by the squeezing among MnO2 nanoparticles during the loading process. This result is in good agreement with the morphology changes (Fig. 5).

The above results demonstrate that MnO2@PET-2 owned interconnected network structures and abundant pore distribution, and MnO2 nanoparticles firmly adhered onto the PET fibers. The tight binding can be ascribed to the thermal bonding among PET fiber and MnO2, and the squeeze effect of the blades on the MnO2 nanoparticles. PET fibers are flexible with high toughness, and MnO2 nanoparticles have a large specific surface area, which facilitates them to fully contact with the fibers. The mixture of PET fiber and MnO2 powder was mixed in the blender by the fast rotating blades, and the friction heat (60 ∼ 70 °C) generated among them made the thermoplastic PET fibers soft, deformative and become partially molten, which efficiently enhanced interfacial adhesion among PET fiber and MnO2 (Fig. 9
a-9c) [42,43]. At the same time, MnO2 powder could be squeezed or even compacted by the blades during the loading process and would be firmly adhered to the fiber surface.

In the light of previous researches, the close binding between PET and MnO2 may also originate from the chemical bonding [44,45]. To know whether the chemical bonding made PET and MnO2 bounded together in this case, attenuation total reflection Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR) analysis was conducted to check the change of the surface functional groups during the loading process (Fig. 10
a). MnO2 exhibited obvious peaks at 3340 cm−1 and 1634 cm−1, which were ascribed to the —OH stretching vibrations of adsorbed water molecules and the —OH bending vibrations [46,47], respectively. Compared with the PET fiber itself, the MnO2@PET-2 also exhibited absorption at 3340 cm−1 and 1634 cm−1. Additionally, no new obvious peaks appeared in MnO2@PET-2, indicating there is no chemical bonding among MnO2 and PET fibers.

The 1H NMR spectrum was further used to probe hydrogen bonds because the formation of hydrogen bonds can cause 1H shifts [48]. Fig. 10 b shows the 1H MAS NMR spectra of MnO2@PET-2 and MnO2, and a significant signal occurring around 3 ppm in the spectra of MnO2@PET-2 and MnO2 can be due to the surface hydroxyl groups of MnO2 (Mn-OH) [49,50]. Compared with MnO2, a distinct shift could be observed for MnO2@PET-2, indicating the presence of hydrogen bonds. Based on the weak intensity of Mn-OH, it can be concluded that the interaction force between MnO2 and PET is partly attributed to hydrogen bonding. Thus, the binding of MnO2 onto PET fibers were mostly caused by the friction heat, which made the thermoplastic PET fibers become viscous and bound MnO2 nanoparticles.

Attributed to the efficient ability of MnO2 powder for HCHO oxidation, the MnO2 loaded PET fibers (MnO2@PET) also exhibited great promise for HCHO removal. Fig. 11
a-11b shows the HCHO removal performance of MnO2@PET composites achieved by loading MnO2 twice on the surface of PET fiber with different diameters (7, 15, 20, 30 µm, respectively). All MnO2@PET composites exhibited remarkable capability of HCHO oxidation to CO2. Especially, MnO2@PET-7 µm showed the highest production of CO2 within 160 min, and the reasons probably derived from the maximum loading of MnO2 catalyst attributed to the largest surface area under the same weight. Fig. 11 c-11d demonstrates HCHO elimination property of MnO2@PET-7 µm composites obtained by loading MnO2 different times (1–6 times). Among them, MnO2@PET-2 showed HCHO removal rate of 95.5% and the highest conversion to CO2 (75.5%), which was close to that loaded with six times. This result is better than that of the reported PET fabrics loaded with MnO2 catalysts [35,51], and the conversion to CO2 is significantly higher than that of reported polypropylene (PP) nonwovens supported MnO2 and ZnO [18]. Besides, the HCHO conversion to CO2 had a little difference among different composite samples, and the HCHO removal performance had no significant difference due to the compaction of MnO2 nanoparticles. This result is in good agreement with the morphological analysis in Fig. 5 that MnO2@PET-2 might expose more active sites of MnO2 catalyst, and yet the coverage of active sites of MnO2 catalyst arising from the agglomeration or compaction among MnO2 nanoparticles might occur with the increase of loading times. Hence, MnO2@PET-2 is selected for the following HCHO removal tests.

Regarding economic and environmental sustainability, the materials for HCHO removal are expected to possess a favorable reusable capability. In a static experiment, the six repeated tests were performed with MnO2@PET-2. The results show that the HCHO removal efficiency gradually decreased with the increase of repeated tests and it still reached 68.9% after the sixth repeated test (Fig. 12
a). As explained above, with the progress of HCHO oxidation, the intermediate species (e. g. carbonate and formate species) will gradually accumulate on the surface of the materials. After the intermediate species accumulate to a certain amount, the activity of composite MnO2 material will decrease due to the coverage of active sites. Whether the intermediate species on the catalyst surface can be fast transformed into CO2 and rapidly released is a critical point for the long-term usage or reuse. We regenerated the used MnO2@PET-2 at 60 °C in oven for 120 min, and tested the activity again. As can be seen from the inset of Fig. 12 a, the regenerated MnO2@PET-2 displayed favorable HCHO removal capability, that is 92.5% of HCHO removal rate and 72.0% of HCHO conversion rate. To know the continuous ability of the as-synthesized composite materials to remove HCHO with the concentration close to the real indoor environment, the dynamic test was employed at room temperature. As shown in Fig. 12 b, the MnO2@PET-2 showed stable removal rate as high as 88.2% for 0.3 mg/m3 HCHO flow within 30 h, indicating that MnO2@PET-2 owned superb stability of HCHO oxidation.

In summary, MnO2 nanoparticles with efficient HCHO removal ability were fast and firmly adhered to the surface of PET fiber without binder. The thickness of coated MnO2 particles on the PET fibers was in the range of 0.14–2.19 µm, and the mass ratio of loaded MnO2 to the PET fibers could be as high as 11.8–30 % depending on the loading times. The flexible coating of MnO2 nanoparticles to the PET fibers could be ascribed to the friction-heat and the compaction effect of the rapidly rotating blades. The friction heat made the PET fibers viscous and adhesive to MnO2. The 180 min ultrasonic oscillation test demonstrated most of coated MnO2 nanoparticles firmly adhered to the PET fibers except 10.2 ∼ 10.4 % peeled off in the first 30 min. Both static and dynamic tests demonstrated that as-synthesized MnO2@PET composite materials had favorable HCHO removal performance and easy regenerability at low temperature. Therefore, such a green and facile loading method provides a choice for efficient loading of various nanoparticle catalysts on the polymer fibers.
